name: Punic Empire

fields.foundation: The Punic Empire is more precisely the Carthaginian Empire; its name derives from the Latin Punicus, “Phoenician”. It began as a colony of the Phoenician city of Tyre on the North African coast, traditionally founded in 814 BCE by the Tyrian princess Elissa, known to later tradition as Dido. According to legend, she negotiated with the local king Iarbas for as much land as a single ox-hide could cover, then cut the hide into strips thin enough to encircle the hill of Byrsa, “hide” in Greek, on which Carthage’s citadel was later built. Behind this founding myth lay the Phoenician practice of establishing coastal trading posts across the Mediterranean from the ninth century BCE onwards, driven by Tyre’s need to secure metals, particularly silver and tin, beyond the Levant. Carthage stood on the Tunisian promontory commanding the narrows between Sicily and Africa, the most strategically placed of all Phoenician foundations. Independence from Tyre came gradually over the seventh and sixth centuries BCE, as Assyrian and then Babylonian pressure on the Phoenician homeland weakened ties with the mother city and Carthage assumed leadership of the western Phoenician settlements. The Magonid dynasty, whose founder Mago I is placed around the mid-sixth century BCE, began systematic empire-building. Carthage, until then a trading city, extended its authority over neighbouring Libyan populations, established hegemony over Sardinia, controlled western Sicily and secured the Balearic Islands, a source of mercenaries famous throughout the ancient world for their skill with the sling. Alexander the Great sacked Tyre in 332 BCE, before which some Tyrians had sent their families to safety in Carthage. The eastern mother city was humbled, and Carthage was from then on an independent centre of civilisation in its own right.
fields.socioeconomy: Carthage at its commercial peak was arguably the wealthiest city in the Mediterranean world. Its mercantile economy combined productive agriculture, skilled manufacturing and a maritime trading network extending from the Atlantic coasts of Iberia and Morocco to the ports of the eastern Mediterranean. The agricultural hinterland of northern Tunisia, among the most fertile land of the ancient world, was organised in large estates worked by enslaved labour and by subject Libyan populations paying heavy tribute. Carthaginian farming was advanced enough for the writer Mago to produce an agricultural treatise in twenty-eight books. It was so highly regarded that the Roman Senate ordered its translation into Latin after Carthage’s destruction in 146 BCE, and so kept the manual while obliterating the civilisation that produced it. Carthage protected its commercial network by a policy of maritime exclusivity: the Treaties between Rome and Carthage, the first traditionally dated to 509 BCE and another to 348 BCE, barred Roman and Italian merchants from trading in Carthaginian waters beyond specified limits, protecting Punic monopolies in western Mediterranean and Atlantic trade. The city’s workshops produced purple-dyed textiles using the murex process inherited from Phoenicia, fine metalwork, glass and ceramics that commanded high prices across Mediterranean markets. Silver from the Spanish mines, exploited intensively after the Barcid conquest of southern Iberia beginning in 237 BCE, financed Carthage’s late imperial power. It funded Hannibal’s Italian campaign and long sustained the war against Rome despite Rome’s far larger citizen population and Italian alliance network.
fields.military: The Carthaginian military was built around a professional core of mercenary and allied troops recruited from across the Mediterranean and African worlds, including Numidian cavalry, Balearic slingers, Iberian swordsmen, Gallic warriors, Libyan infantry and Greek technical specialists. Citizen levies supplemented them, as did, from the third century BCE, war elephants drawn from the now-extinct North African forest elephant population. The system followed from Carthage’s commercial ethos: military service was largely bought rather than owed as a civic obligation. Large and diverse forces could be assembled quickly, but their loyalty and cohesion were chronically weak. The Mercenary War of 241–238 BCE showed as much, when unpaid veterans of the First Punic War turned on Carthage itself in a brutal conflict that Gustave Flaubert later fictionalised in Salammbô. The empire’s greatest military achievement was Hannibal Barca’s invasion of Italy during the Second Punic War, beginning with his crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE with some 26,000 surviving troops and a dwindling elephant corps. Three crushing Roman defeats followed: the Trebia in 218 BCE, Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE and above all Cannae in 216 BCE, where Hannibal’s double envelopment of a Roman army of perhaps 80,000 men killed an estimated 47,000–70,000 in a single afternoon. It was one of the worst defeats in Roman history, and the battle is still studied today as a tactical masterpiece. Naval power mattered as much. Carthage’s fleets of quinqueremes dominated the western Mediterranean until Rome built its first great fleet by copying a captured Carthaginian warship, devised the corvus boarding bridge and challenged that supremacy. The loss of sea control in the First Punic War proved irreversible.
fields.governance: Carthage’s constitution was admired enough in antiquity for Aristotle to discuss it in his Politics alongside those of Sparta and Crete. It was the only non-Greek state he examined at length, and he judged it among the best-ordered of his age. The government combined monarchical, oligarchic and democratic elements in a mixed constitution. Executive authority lay with two annually elected suffetes, magistrates whose title shares a Semitic root with the Hebrew shofet, “judge”, who presided over civil administration, while military command was held separately by generals. A Council of Elders, a senate of wealthy aristocrats perhaps several hundred strong, was the principal body for deliberation and policy. The Court of the One Hundred and Four, whose precise composition and powers remain debated, held officials and generals to account. It could punish unsuccessful commanders severely and even crucify them, a sanction that encouraged effectiveness but may have discouraged strategic risk-taking; Aristotle likened this body to the Spartan ephors. Popular assemblies of the citizens held residual authority, deciding matters when the suffetes and the council disagreed, and their influence grew in the later third century BCE. The empire’s provinces in North Africa, Sicily, Sardinia and Iberia were managed through governors and local elites with varying degrees of autonomy. Libyan subjects were more heavily taxed and controlled than the Phoenician settlements, a difference that caused recurring unrest. It helps to explain why Numidian and Iberian allies, most prominently the Numidian prince Masinissa, defected to Rome once Carthaginian power began to fail during the Second Punic War.
fields.impact: Carthage’s impact on the ancient Mediterranean world was great but has been obscured by the completeness of its destruction. The Romans razed the city and enslaved its surviving population, and the later, unsubstantiated legend that they salted the earth reflects how total that erasure was. As a result, what Punic civilisation contributed reached later ages almost entirely through Greek and Roman sources written by its adversaries. Carthaginian seafarers ranged far beyond the Mediterranean. Hanno the Navigator sailed down the Atlantic coast of Africa, probably in the fifth century BCE, and may have reached as far as Sierra Leone or even Cameroon according to competing interpretations of his surviving periplus; it was the most ambitious known exploration of that coast before the Portuguese voyages of the fifteenth century CE. Himilco’s voyage northward along the Atlantic coasts of Europe sought access to the tin trade of the north-west. Carthaginian agricultural science, preserved through the Roman translation of Mago's treatise, influenced Mediterranean farming for centuries. Punic urban planning, religious architecture and religious practice persisted in North Africa, Iberia and Sardinia long after political Carthage ceased to exist. That practice included the controversial tophet sanctuaries, whose remains have produced sustained debate over whether they attest child sacrifice or infant burial. The Punic language was still spoken in North Africa in the time of St Augustine. The Punic Wars compelled Rome to build a permanent navy and to develop provincial government, beginning with Sicily, and so turned it from an Italian power into a Mediterranean empire.
fields.decline: The Punic Empire was destroyed by strategic overextension, the limitations of its mercenary military system, the loss of its commercial and territorial assets in three devastating wars with Rome, and finally the deliberate decision of the Roman Senate to eliminate Carthage altogether rather than merely as a competitor. The First Punic War of 264–241 BCE, which began over conflicting interests in Sicily, lasted twenty-three years and ended with Carthage’s naval defeat at the Battle of the Aegates Islands. Carthage had to surrender Sicily, its richest overseas possession, and pay an indemnity of 3,200 talents of silver over ten years. Rome opportunistically seized Sardinia and Corsica in 238–237 BCE during the Mercenary War, in breach of the spirit of the peace, and added a further indemnity. The resentment this caused drove the Barcid family to build a Spanish empire, both as financial compensation and as preparation for renewed conflict. Hannibal’s campaign in the Second Punic War of 218–201 BCE came close to its strategic objective, the dissolution of Rome’s Italian alliance network. But most of Rome’s Latin and Italian allies stayed loyal even after Cannae, Rome adopted the delaying strategy associated with Fabius Maximus, and the Scipio family, above all Publius Cornelius Scipio, destroyed Carthaginian power in Spain. Hannibal could win battles but not the war without reinforcements and siege equipment that Carthage failed to provide. Recalled to Africa, he was defeated by Scipio at Zama in 202 BCE. The final destruction was a matter of political will rather than military necessity. Cato the Elder is said to have ended his speeches with the declaration that Carthage must be destroyed (Carthago delenda est), and the Third Punic War of 149–146 BCE was a siege of a city that posed little real threat. It ended when Scipio Aemilianus’s forces stormed Carthage after six days of street fighting and razed it. Tradition holds that the city burned for seventeen days, and an estimated 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery.
fields.summary: The Punic Empire was destroyed so completely that its commercial and constitutional culture, among the most developed of the ancient Mediterranean, survives chiefly in the literature of its destroyers. Carthage is an example of what is lost when the victors alone write the record.
fields.teaser: Carthage, founded by Phoenician settlers, became one of the ancient Mediterranean's greatest trading powers. Its three Punic Wars with Rome had lasting consequences for Western civilisation.
fields.t0: Carthage, a Phoenician colony of Tyre in Tunisia, built a trading empire across the western Mediterranean.
fields.t1: Its fleets, mercenary armies and Hannibal's invasion of Italy made it Rome's greatest rival for over a century.
fields.t2: Three Punic Wars stripped it of Sicily, Spain and its navy; Rome razed the city in 146 BCE and enslaved its survivors.
fields.dyk: After destroying Carthage, the Roman Senate ordered the farming treatise of the Carthaginian writer Mago, in twenty-eight books, to be translated into Latin.
